summary: Aaron wears the inscribed gold plate on his forehead. A hard forehead can express both the people’s refusal to listen and the firmness Ezekiel needs to speak to them. The related-looking noun מִצְחָה names a piece of leg armour.

senses.definition: The front of the head above the eyes, a visible place for an inscription, mark or blemish.

evidence.note: The gold plate fastened to Aaron’s turban rests on his forehead.
The man in linen is told to mark the foreheads of those who grieve over Jerusalem’s abominations.
The priests see the outbreak on Uzziah’s forehead as he stands in the sanctuary.

senses.gloss: forehead as an image of defiance or resolve
senses.definition: In descriptions of someone facing another, the brow can express open shamelessness, resistance to correction or the resolve to withstand opposition.

evidence.note: The image of a prostitute’s forehead is explained by the accusation that Judah refuses to feel shame.
A bronze forehead and an iron neck portray the people’s stubbornness.
Israel’s hard forehead is paired with hardness of heart and refusal to hear.
Yahweh makes Ezekiel’s forehead harder than flint and tells him to face the rebellious people without fear.

senses.definition: A protective covering worn on the lower legs.

evidence.note: The inventory of Goliath’s armour locates the bronze piece on his legs.

evidence.locator: M02303, Targum Pseudo-Jonathan Genesis 4:8, with M02302

note: Jewish Aramaic has a matching word for the forehead, but the attestation leaves inheritance and borrowing open. The explanation of the greave as covering the front of the leg suits its position in 1 Samuel 17:6. The verse gives no account of how the piece got its name.
